1914-1920

Caption This

America and the Great War

13

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Wilson’s “Peace with Honor” truck

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 21. A truck covered in flags and big signs sits on a city street. Two men are with it. The signs say “Vote for Wilson” and “Peace with honor. Prosperity. Preparedness.” One sign asks, “Who keeps us out of war?” Norton says it comes from the 1916 campaign.

Heads up: Real people are in this photo. Aim your joke at the truck, the flags, or the pile of signs. Never joke about the men in the photo or about anyone who died in the war.

  • Read the tall sign in the middle. What does it ask about war?
  • Why would a campaign put “Peace” and “Preparedness” on the same truck?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: U-boatsZimmermann telegram
Image 2 of 5

“Don’t read American history. Make it!”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color poster from the first page of Norton Ch. 21. A sailor in a white uniform points toward ships far away and talks to a young man in a suit, who is holding a newspaper. Above them, a woman in a star-covered dress holds a flag and a sword. The words say, “The Navy needs you! Don’t read American history. Make it!”

Heads up: This poster was made to get people to join the war. Aim your joke at the newspaper, the giant flag, or the idea of “making history” by joining up. Never joke about sailors or soldiers who were hurt or killed, or about any group of people.

  • The man in the suit is holding a newspaper. What is the sailor telling him to do instead?
  • Where is the sailor pointing? What is out there?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 3 of 5

Armistice Night in New York

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painting from Norton Ch. 21. A huge crowd fills a street at night, and the sky is full of waving flags from many countries, including American, British, and French flags. Norton says the artist, George Luks, painted the joy on the night the fighting ended.

Heads up: This painting shows a party at the end of a war that killed millions. Aim your joke at the flags, the huge crowd, or how loud the night must have been. Never joke about soldiers who died or families who lost someone.

  • How many different flags can you find? Why would flags from so many countries be flying?
  • Look at the crowd. What mood do you see?

Image 4 of 5

The Big Four at Versailles

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 21. Four men in dark suits stand outside a doorway of the palace at Versailles. Norton lists them, left to right, as David Lloyd George, Vittorio Orlando, Georges Clemenceau, and Woodrow Wilson. The two men on the left lean in and talk. Wilson, on the right, is smiling.

Heads up: These are real leaders, and the photo shows their faces. Aim your joke at the situation: four men on a doorstep deciding the future of the world. Never joke about how anyone looks, or about the people who died in the war.

  • Look at the four men. Who is talking, who is listening, and who is looking at the camera?
  • Norton says Germany was not invited to these talks. What might the four men decide without Germany in the room?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 5 of 5

Women vote for the first time

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 21. Women stand behind wooden ballot boxes and hand their ballots to an election worker. Several of them smile. Norton says these are women of New York City’s East Side voting for the first time in the presidential election of 1920.

Heads up: Real people are in this photo, and several are smiling. Aim your joke at the ballot boxes, the curtains, or the stack of ballots. Never joke about the women, about women voting, or about anyone who was kept from voting.

  • Look at the faces. What mood do you see? What is the woman in the middle holding?
  • Why do you think reporters took photos of women voting that day?
